objectives: Read controlled sentences containing taught short /o/ words accurately.
Identify people, actions and details stated in sentences.
Use text evidence to answer literal comprehension questions.
Monitor short /o/ decoding while maintaining sentence meaning.
concepts: Literal questions can be answered from explicitly stated sentence information.
Rereading supports both decoding accuracy and meaning.

definitions.definition: Understanding information directly stated in a text.
A specific word or phrase that supports an answer.
A sentence built mainly from previously taught sound-spelling patterns.

workedExamples: “Tom has a mop.” → Who? Tom. What? A mop.
“The dog is hot.” → What is hot? The dog.
If hot is read as hat, return to the middle vowel and decode again.
commonMistakes: Answering from memory rather than the sentence.
Ignoring the word that states the object.
revisionPoints: Who? What? Which detail? Point to the supporting word.

conceptual: Identify the word that answers a question.
higherOrderThinking: Explain which words provide evidence for an answer.
mixedReview: Decode and answer literal comprehension questions.

formulaOrFactBank: Literal answer = information stated in the sentence
weakTopicRevision: Point to the exact evidence before saying the answer.

outcomes: Learner reads controlled short /o/ sentences with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner identifies stated people and objects with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner answers literal detail questions using text evidence.
Learner self-corrects a short /o/ decoding error and rereads for meaning.

questions.question: Read: “Tom has a mop.” Who has a mop?
Read: “Tom has a mop.” What does Tom have?
Read: “The dog is hot.” What is hot?
Read: “The dog is hot.” Which word describes the dog?
Read: “Tom got a pot.” What did Tom get?
Read: “Tom got a pot.” Who got the pot?
Read: “The dog got hot.” What happened to the dog?
Which word tells what Tom has in “Tom has a mop”?
Which sentence means Tom has a pot?
A learner reads “hot” as “hat.” What should they check?
options: The middle vowel o versus a

questions.question: Read: “Tom has a mop. The dog is hot.” Which statement is supported?
options: Tom has a mop and the dog is hot.

questions.question: What should a learner do after reading a controlled sentence?
options: Reread and check that the meaning makes sense

questions.question: Which word has short /o/ in “The dog is hot”?
Why is text evidence useful?
options: It shows which words support the answer
It removes the need to read

questions.question: What is the main goal of this lesson?
options: Read controlled short /o/ sentences accurately and answer literal questions
